title: Plain as You Like
blurb: A junior clerk unties two strands of umbrella trouble on a quiet set of steps, and the man at the centre of it stops breathing.

blocks.text: Noon on the Lantry Steps, and there is not a breath of wind.

Every umbrella within ten metres of the man with the sandwich turns inside out at once. Pop, pop, pop, a whole row of black tulips opening the wrong way. A woman in a yellow mac shrieks, then laughs. The man keeps eating.
I hold my bob out over him on its silk. It gives a half-turn, as if it has changed its mind, then circles twice and settles, crooked, towards his chest.
Item: the man on the steps is the anchor. Item: two strands, nuisance weight. Item: a half-turn means something nested, and nested knots stay put unless they were tied as slips. Item: this is easy.
The man glances at the fid on my belt. "Careful with that spike."
I beam at him, because I have waited four years to beam at somebody on a warrant. "Good afternoon! I'm Ila Brandt, from the Bureau of—"
"Of Lost Umbrellas, I should think," he says. His voice is courtly and a little worn, like a good coat that has been out in a lot of weather. "How do you do."

Nobody calls a fid a spike. Not any more. I have read every training manual Registry owns, and the last one that said "spike" was printed before I was born. I tuck that away with the other odd thing about today.
The other odd thing is the warrant itself.

This morning, at the Registry counter where I have spent four years filing other people's repairs, my supervisor put an emergency warrant in my hand and said, "Don't get excited." I got excited. It came from an anonymous complaint about umbrellas on the Lantry Steps, which is exactly the kind of nuisance a Registry Clerk is allowed to clear. A clerk may untie up to two strands under an emergency warrant, and not one strand more, and two is exactly my reach after four years on the training frames. So that part was fine.

What I noticed, while I was signing for it, was the countersignature. Field Allocation. Senior Knotter Vosper's section. Field Allocation does not countersign anonymous complaints. I decided that meant somebody upstairs thought I was ready, and I decided not to ask in case they changed their mind.

The tram driver who brought me down the hill was called Wilf. I asked him at the first stop, and then told him where I was going and why. When I got off I said, "Thank you, Wilf," and he said, "Mind the puddles, Bureau," and I very nearly floated down the steps.
Now there is rain down my collar and a puddle in my left shoe, and none of it matters.
The man has a leather case beside him on the step, the kind with brass corners. Gold letters on the lid say L. PARGETER, PIANO TUNER.
"Mr Pargeter?"
He hums three notes of something under his breath, then says, "The very same."

The flower seller at the foot of the steps has been watching all of this over her buckets. She is about sixty, in a fleece the colour of a postbox, and she leans out to me as if we are already friends.
"You won't shift him, love," she says. "He's here every day at noon. Same step, same sandwich. Cheese and pickle."
"Every day?" I go down two steps so we can talk properly. "I'm Ila. What's your name?"

"Bernadette. Bernie." She points at him with a bunch of daffodils. "Every day since my mum had this pitch, and I've had it twenty years myself. Thirty years, near enough, he's been eating his lunch on that step. You could time the trams by him."
"Thirty years," I say. "That's lovely."

It is lovely. It is also exactly how a worn knot forms. The rulebook says it plainly: a pattern repeated without a single change, year after year, until the world starts bending round it. The umbrellas are the bend. And here it is in front of me in the rain, eating a cheese and pickle sandwich.
I swing him again, slowly, to be sure. The half-turn. Then two circles. Then still.

The warrant has a checklist on the back, and I go down it with my pencil: anchor, count, keeper, reach. There is no box for a half-turn. I know what a half-turn means, though, word for word. A nested knot shows only as a hesitation before the count, and the bob counts the outer knot alone. Lifting the outer knot to count the one inside is Second Class work, and I am not Second Class. I am not any class at all.

But I do not need to count it. I only need to know what happens to it. Untying an outer knot releases the knot inside only if the inside one was tied as a slip. Otherwise the inner knot stays exactly where it is and becomes the outer one. And a slip is something a knotter ties on purpose, to come loose when somebody wants it to.
Nobody ties a slip on a man eating his lunch.

So whatever is inside will stay put, and I will write it up in the remarks, and somebody with a Second Class licence can come and count it properly next week. I feel very sensible about this. I feel like a field knotter.
"Mr Pargeter," I say, "I'm going to untie the knot on these steps. You won't feel a thing. The umbrellas will just stop."
He looks at me for a long moment. Rain is beading on the brim of his hat.
"Must you?" he says.
"Somebody complained, I'm afraid. It's a public nuisance."
"Somebody always does." He takes another bite of his sandwich and looks out at the river. "Well. You'll do as you think best, Miss Brandt. People generally do."

I take the docket card out of my satchel and tie it to my fid by its string. Then I sign it. Ila Brandt, in my own hand, before the fid goes in. That makes me the keeper. When the knot comes free, its slack will dwell here on the steps, a minute for each strand, and then fall on me, somewhere in the next twenty-four hours, against the grain of whatever I happen to want. Two strands is nothing. A missed tram. A spilled tea. The Porters take heavier than this every day for their day rate.
I kneel on the wet step beside him. Bernie shoos a pigeon off the railing so nobody can bump my elbow. "Go on, love," she says. "Show us."
The fid goes in.

It does not go into Mr Pargeter. It goes into the air just in front of his chest, where the bob pulled, and the brass meets something that is not there and is. Four years of frame drills in the Registry basement, and it feels exactly the same. That surprises me.

The first strand is the weather, I think: a slow, sulky pull like wet rope. I work it with the point of the fid, patient, not hurrying, because an interruption would snarl the whole knot and then it would misfire on everyone on these steps. Nobody interrupts me. The steps are quiet except for the rain on the canvas of Bernie's stall.
The first strand lets go.
The second is quicker, lighter, a little springy, like a habit. It comes free in my hand at the end of the second minute, and the knot is gone.
Above me the woman in the yellow mac puts her umbrella up, and it stays the right way out. She looks at it as if it has done something clever.
"There," I say, sitting back on my heels. "All done, Mr Pargeter. You won't—"
He does not finish my sentence.
The sandwich slides off his knee onto the step. He tips sideways against the railing, slowly, like a man getting comfortable, and his face goes the colour of the stone.
"Mr Pargeter?"
Nothing. I put two fingers to his neck and there is nothing there either. His lips are going grey.

I get him flat on the landing. My hands find the middle of his chest through his cardigan, one on top of the other, and I push, hard, the way the Bureau's first-aid course taught us. His chest gives under my hands far more than I expected. I push again. Again.
And I am frightened, so frightened my teeth hurt, and I start pulling in everyone I can see.
"You in the green coat," I say to a woman on the step above. "Kneel down and hold his head. Keep it still and keep it straight. Please."
She kneels. Her hands are cold and steady either side of his face.
"You with the dog. Find me a phone. Ring for an ambulance and tell them a man's heart has stopped on the Lantry Steps."
A man in a flat cap, with a wet spaniel on a lead, already has his phone out.
"Bernie. You with the flowers. Watch the tram stop for the ambulance and wave it down when it comes."
Bernie says nothing, just goes, buckets and all, and stands at the kerb with her arm half raised.

I keep pushing. I do not know how long. My arms burn, then go past burning into something duller. The man with the dog says, "They say twelve minutes. Twelve minutes, they're saying," and the woman in the green coat says, "Keep going, you're doing it, keep going," and I keep going.
I unpicked two strands of umbrella. That is all I did. Umbrellas do not stop a man's heart.
Then three things happen that nobody asked for.
A woman steps out of the tram queue with her coat open over blue hospital scrubs. "Cardiac nurse," she says. "Off shift. Don't stop." She is kneeling beside me before I can answer.

A man in a council jacket, who has been standing in the tram shelter with a screwdriver this whole time, turns round with a green box in his hands. He has just fixed the bracket for it to the shelter wall. The box says DEFIBRILLATOR in white letters. He looks at it, and at us, and runs.

And at the foot of the steps, where the road meets the river, an ambulance is already stopped at the lights. Its blue lights are off. It is on its way back from somewhere else. Bernie sees it and starts waving both arms.
I stare at all of it with my hands still on his chest.

"I didn't ask for any of that," I say, out loud, to nobody in particular. "I asked for a head held and a phone and somebody to watch the tram stop. I didn't ask for a nurse or a defibrillator or an ambulance. That's three things nobody asked for."
"Then don't knock them," the nurse says. "Hands off a second."
She has scissors from somewhere. She cuts his shirt and cardigan straight up the front, and then she stops for half a breath.
There is a scar across his chest. Not a surgeon's line. A wide, pale, puckered band from one side of his ribs to the other, as if something very heavy lay across him once.
"That's a crush injury," she says. "That's old. Years old." She presses the pads on, quick and flat. "This heart should have quit years ago. Something's been keeping it going."
Something has been keeping it going.
The half-turn. The thing inside the umbrella knot, that I did not count because I was not allowed to, that I decided would stay put because nobody ties a slip on a man eating his lunch.
Somebody did.
"I'm wrong," I say. My voice comes out high and odd. "I'm wrong. The inside one wasn't staying put. It was holding him."

The nurse does not ask what I mean. The green box speaks in a calm, flat voice about analysing rhythm and standing clear, and we all stand clear, and it does not shock him. On its little screen there is a line, and the line is flat.
The paramedics are on the steps now, two of them, with a stretcher and a bag. One takes over from the nurse. The nurse goes with them, talking fast in words I do not know.
I stand on the landing with my hands held out in front of me, because I do not know where else to put them.

They lift him in. One of the paramedics puts the piano tuner's case on the stretcher by his feet, which is a kind thing to do. As the doors swing shut I see the monitor inside, a green line crawling flat across the screen, and I hear someone in there say, quietly, "I'm sorry."
Then the doors close, and the blue lights come on, and the ambulance goes.
The umbrellas on the Lantry Steps stay the right way out. Somebody's spaniel shakes itself. Everybody is looking at me.
I turn to the woman in the green coat. "What's your name?"
"Hester."
"Thank you, Hester. You held him so still."
The man with the dog. "Colin," he says. "And she's Biscuit."
"Thank you, Colin. Thank you, Biscuit."
Bernie, at the kerb, with rain running off her fleece. "You know mine, love."
"Thank you, Bernie."
The man in the council jacket is called Ray, and I thank him too. The nurse, I realise, never told me hers, and the ambulance is already over the bridge.
Then I pick up my fid from the step where I left it. The docket is still tied to it, wet now, my name running a little at the edges.

I swing the steps once before I go, because that is on the checklist. The bob is straight and still. Nothing here. No umbrella knot, no half-turn, nothing to tell anyone what was inside it, or who put it there.
My own two strands have not fallen yet. They are coming, somewhere in the next twenty-four hours, and I cannot make myself care.
I take the tram back up the hill to Tallow Row. It is not Wilf driving.

In Registry the radiators are ticking and nobody looks up, because nobody looks up in Registry. I sit at my desk with my wet coat still on and write it all down in my best handwriting. The anchor. The half-turn. The time the knot came free. The time his heart stopped.
My supervisor reads it over my shoulder, which she has never done before.
"Outcome," she says, tapping the box.
"I think I killed him."
She considers this. "There isn't a box for that," she says. "Put 'see remarks.'"

So I put "see remarks". And in the remarks I write his name as it was on his case, L. Pargeter, piano tuner, and that he ate his lunch on the Lantry Steps at noon for thirty years, near enough. It seems important that somebody writes that down.
I stay late. I do not want to go home and be asked how my day was. At six I give up and go down the main stairs into the lobby with the wet docket in my pocket.
Stan on the front desk has his hand over the telephone. "Miss Brandt," he says, in the voice he uses for deliveries that will not fit through the door. "Gentleman for you."
The gentleman is standing on the front-desk carpet, dripping.

He is wearing a cardigan cut up the front and buttoned back together wrong, a coat that is not his, and a white plastic hospital band on his left wrist. He has his leather case with the brass corners. He has his hat.
He is Mr Pargeter. He is alive.
He takes his hat off to me, very courteously, as though we are being introduced at a dance.
"They said your name on the ambulance radio, Miss Brandt," he says, "while they were restarting my heart. Ila Brandt. Plain as you like. I should very much like to know why."
